1	\section{Experiments}
2	
3	\subsection{Setup}
4	
5	We evaluate on synthetic and semi-synthetic data generating processes (DGPs); full specifications appear in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.
6	The synthetic DGP generates $N{=}5{,}000$ observations from a randomized trial with $K \in \{2, 4\}$ subgroups, controlled CATE heterogeneity $\Delta\tau$, and subgroup-specific symmetric misclassification rates with heterogeneity $\Delta\pi$.
7	Expert labels ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{50, \ldots, 2000\}$) are a simple random sample with true $Z$ observed; each configuration is repeated for 100 Monte Carlo runs.
8	The semi-synthetic DGP samples $N{=}5{,}000$ tweets from TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, defining $K{=}4$ subgroups by crossing hashtag presence and text length (unbalanced: 39\%/38\%/12\%/11\%), with misclassification rates $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$ reflecting empirical evidence that text features degrade LLM accuracy~\cite{ashwin2025bias}.
9	
10	We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup MLE without pooling), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
11	For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
12	Our Global baseline is equivalent to PPI/DSL~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,egami2024dsl} applied with a pooled (homogeneous) error rate; Stratified MLE corresponds to per-subgroup DSL without hierarchical shrinkage.
13	EC-HTE extends this by borrowing strength across subgroups via hierarchical Bayesian estimation.
14	Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
15	Real-data validation on hate speech detection confirms $\Delta\pi = 0.117$ across text-feature subgroups (Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}).
16	The heterogeneity pattern persists across six OpenAI models spanning three generations (Appendix~\ref{app:multilm}) and four open-source LLMs in the 7B--9B parameter range (Section~\ref{sec:multilm_opensource}).
17	EC-HTE maintains $\geq$94.5\% coverage under up to 50\% subgroup misspecification noise (Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).
18	When empirical asymmetric confusion matrices from the GPT-4.1 pilot are used directly, a subgroup with FNR~$\approx 0.5$ causes EC-HTE to underperform global correction at all budgets (Appendix~\ref{app:semireal}).
19	
20	\subsection{Bias Mechanism Verification}
21	\label{sec:bias_mechanism}
22	
23	The bias decomposition identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) predicts that global correction introduces bias proportional to $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ at the subgroup level.
24	We verify this identity empirically across 520 configurations spanning $K \in \{2,4\}$, two misclassification regimes, and six expert budget levels.
25	Regressing observed subgroup bias on the predicted $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product yields $R^2 = 0.994$ for $K{=}2$ and $R^2 = 0.974$ for $K{=}4$; the residual variance reflects MC sampling noise rather than model misspecification, since Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} is an exact identity at the population level ($R^2 \geq 0.976$ even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$; Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}).
26	In 50\% of configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta_c{=}0$ rows where bias is zero by construction), global correction produces larger absolute bias than the naive estimator.
27	The damage concentrates in low-$\pi$ subgroups: among subgroups where $\pi_s < \bar{\pi}$, global correction increases bias in 84.6\% of cases.
28	Maximum observed amplification reaches 2.86$\times$ (K=2) and 2.41$\times$ (K=4) relative to the naive estimator.
29	Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ amplification surface across the parameter grid.

32	\centering
33	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig2_heatmap.pdf}
34	\caption{Bias amplification under global correction across the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ parameter grid ($K{=}2$). (a) Low-error subgroup: global correction always helps (ratio $< 1$). (b) High-error subgroup: when $\Delta\pi > 0.12$ (dashed line), global correction \emph{increases} bias relative to the naive estimator (hatched region), with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$.}
35	\label{fig:heatmap}
36	\end{figure*}
37	
38	\subsection{EC-HTE Evaluation}
39	\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}
40	
41	Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.
42	In the synthetic DGP with $K{=}2$ subgroups and extreme misclassification heterogeneity, HB EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 (global) to 0.011 (a 5.4$\times$ reduction) while maintaining nominal coverage (0.95) and comparable RMSE (0.093 vs.\ 0.099).
43	The advantage persists at $K{=}4$: EC-HTE achieves $|\text{bias}|{=}0.009$ versus 0.056 for global (6.2$\times$ reduction), though with a small RMSE penalty (0.127 vs.\ 0.125).
44	Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$), methods converge: EC-HTE and global achieve comparable bias ($p > 0.05$; Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}).
45	In the semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment ($N{=}5{,}000$, $K{=}4$), global correction achieves the lowest $|\text{bias}|$ (0.023), while EC-HTE attains 0.027 with higher RMSE (0.225 vs.\ 0.124), consistent with moderate $\Delta\pi{=}0.20$ and unbalanced subgroup sizes (Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}).
46	
47	\paragraph{CausalForest K-dependence.}
48	When the downstream estimator is a CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, the bias mechanism operates with amplified magnitude.
49	At $K{=}4$/extreme/$n{=}500$, EC-HTE Forest reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.191 (global) to 0.040, a 4.8$\times$ improvement with dramatically better coverage (0.91 vs.\ 0.58).

61	\midrule

82	\subsection{Diagnostic Criterion}
83	\label{sec:diagnostic}
84	
85	Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction increases bias in subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, where $\delta_s = \pi_s - \bar{\pi}$.
86	This condition depends only on per-subgroup misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample, breaking the circular dependency that would arise if the diagnostic required CATE estimates.
87	Since the Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} score is a deterministic function of per-subgroup misclassification rates, a threshold classifier achieves AUC = 0.87 at the subgroup level for predicting whether global correction increases bias relative to the naive estimator.
88	At the setting level, the condition achieves AUC = 0.89 (vs.\ 0.47 for the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product), because it identifies settings where \emph{any} subgroup is harmed.
89	Figure~\ref{fig:roc} (Appendix) shows the ROC curve.
90	
91	\paragraph{Recommended workflow.}
92	\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
93	\item Collect $n \geq 25K / P(Z_{\text{minority}})$ stratified expert labels (e.g., $n \geq 500$ for $K{=}4$, $P(Z{=}1){=}0.2$); compute per-subgroup $\pi_s$ and $\bar{\pi}$.
94	\item Verify (a)~$n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ and (b)~worst-subgroup $\max(\text{FPR}, \text{FNR}) < 0.5$; if either fails, use global correction.
95	\item If any subgroup satisfies $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}), apply EC-HTE; apply PPCI regardless for outcome error (Section~\ref{sec:ppci}).
96	\end{enumerate}

99	\label{sec:budget}

102	Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$), EC-HTE never achieves lower RMSE than global at any budget.
103	HB partial pooling improves over stratified MLE in 21 of 24 configurations, with the two estimators converging by $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$.
104	
105	\subsection{PPCI Complementarity and Estimator Robustness}
106	\label{sec:ppci}
107	
108	EC-HTE composes with PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} for settings where both covariate misclassification and outcome model error are present: EC-HTE+PPCI reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 ($z{=}0$, DGP~C), and the corrected pseudo-outcomes are compatible with other CATE estimators (R-learner bias reduction: 89\%; Appendix~\ref{app:ppci},~\ref{app:rlearner}).

\subsection{EC-HTE Evaluation}
\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.
In the synthetic DGP with $K{=}2$ subgroups and extreme misclassification heterogeneity, HB EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 (global) to 0.011 (a 5.4$\times$ reduction) while maintaining nominal coverage (0.95) and comparable RMSE (0.093 vs.\ 0.099).

\subsection{Diagnostic Criterion}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction increases bias in subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, where $\delta_s = \pi_s - \bar{\pi}$.
This condition depends only on per-subgroup misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample, breaking the circular dependency that would arise if the diagnostic required CATE estimates.
Since the Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} score is a deterministic function of per-subgroup misclassification rates, a threshold classifier achieves AUC = 0.87 at the subgroup level for predicting whether global correction increases bias relative to the naive estimator.
At the setting level, the condition achieves AUC = 0.89 (vs.\ 0.47 for the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product), because it identifies settings where \emph{any} subgroup is harmed.

\paragraph{Recommended workflow.}
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item Collect $n \geq 25K / P(Z_{\text{minority}})$ stratified expert labels (e.g., $n \geq 500$ for $K{=}4$, $P(Z{=}1){=}0.2$); compute per-subgroup $\pi_s$ and $\bar{\pi}$.
\item Verify (a)~$n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ and (b)~worst-subgroup $\max(\text{FPR}, \text{FNR}) < 0.5$; if either fails, use global correction.
\item If any subgroup satisfies $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}), apply EC-HTE; apply PPCI regardless for outcome error (Section~\ref{sec:ppci}).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Expert Budget Analysis}
\label{sec:budget}

The crossover point at which EC-HTE achieves lower RMSE than global correction is $n_{\text{expert}} = 250$ for $K{=}2$/extreme and $n_{\text{expert}} = 1000$ for $K{=}4$/extreme (Figure~\ref{fig:budget} in the Appendix).
Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$), EC-HTE never achieves lower RMSE than global at any budget.
HB partial pooling improves over stratified MLE in 21 of 24 configurations, with the two estimators converging by $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$.

\subsection{PPCI Complementarity and Estimator Robustness}
\label{sec:ppci}

EC-HTE composes with PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} for settings where both covariate misclassification and outcome model error are present: EC-HTE+PPCI reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 ($z{=}0$, DGP~C), and the corrected pseudo-outcomes are compatible with other CATE estimators (R-learner bias reduction: 89\%; Appendix~\ref{app:ppci},~\ref{app:rlearner}).

\subsection{Open-Source Multi-LLM Validation}
\label{sec:multilm_opensource}

To verify that misclassification heterogeneity and EC-HTE's correction generalize beyond proprietary APIs, we annotate 500 TweetEval sentiment tweets with four open-source LLMs: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B-IT.
Each model independently classifies tweets using a 3-class prompt (positive/neutral/negative); we define a balanced binary label $Z{=}1$ if the true label $\geq 1$ (neutral or positive vs.\ negative), yielding $P(Z{=}1) \approx 0.65$.
Per-subgroup confusion matrices are estimated directly from each model's annotations against gold labels.
The EC-HTE pipeline---HB confusion matrix estimation followed by CausalForestDML---is identical to the synthetic experiments in Table~\ref{tab:main_results}.
All four models exhibit subgroup-heterogeneous misclassification ($\Delta\pi \in [0.125, 0.165]$, $K{=}4$), with consistent subgroup error rankings across architectures (Table~\ref{tab:multilm_cm}).
Correction improves 95\% CI coverage from 0.714 (naive average) to 0.941 ($+$22.7 percentage points, $K{=}2$, $n_{\text{expert}}{=}1{,}000$), restoring near-nominal inference across all four models.
Under the moderate $\Delta\pi$ observed in these real LLM annotations, global correction suffices for RMSE.
Stratified correction achieves lower RMSE than the naive estimator only at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1{,}000$ ($K{=}2$); global correction achieves comparable or lower RMSE than HB EC-HTE at all budgets under this moderate heterogeneity, consistent with the budget guidelines in Section~\ref{sec:budget}.
Full per-model results appear in Appendix~\ref{app:multilm_opensource}.

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:intro}
3	
4	Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
5	Yet these annotations are not uniformly accurate.
6	\citet{ashwin2025bias} document that LLM misclassification rates vary by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups defined by refugee status, gender, and education level.
7	In a pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% binary accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$), within the range assumed in our synthetic DGPs ($\Delta\pi = 0.05$--$0.20$).
8	When such annotations serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, subgroup-specific errors propagate directly into conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
9	The resulting bias is not random noise that averages out; it is structured by the same demographic axes that define the research question.
10	Standard correction procedures, which estimate a single confusion matrix and apply its inverse uniformly, cannot account for this heterogeneity.
11	
12	We formalize this problem and discover a previously unrecognized bias mechanism.
13	When a pooled confusion matrix is applied to correct subgroup CATEs, it misattributes error across subgroups with an exact product form: the bias in subgroup $s$ equals $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$, where $\delta_s$ is the deviation from the pooled error rate and $\Delta\tau$ is the CATE heterogeneity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}).
14	This is not a bound but an exact population-level identity, verified empirically with $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $R^2 = 0.974$ ($K{=}4$).
15	A direct consequence is that global correction can be worse than no correction at all: in 50\% of our experimental configurations, global correction increases absolute bias relative to the naive estimator, with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest).
16	Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE) addresses this through hierarchical Bayesian estimation of subgroup-stratified confusion matrices combined with CausalForestDML, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.011 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$).
17	The bias decomposition identity also yields a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}): a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction will fail (AUC = 0.87), so practitioners can decide whether stratified correction is warranted before estimating any treatment effects.
18	EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, global correction suffices and EC-HTE's variance cost is not justified (Figure~\ref{fig:bias_mechanism}).
19	
20	This problem matters because subgroup CATEs inform resource allocation decisions: which communities benefit most from policy interventions, where programs should be targeted, and how reforms affect different groups.
21	Biased CATE estimates can reverse the sign of apparent treatment heterogeneity, leading practitioners to allocate resources away from communities that benefit most.
22	The failure mode is subtle: a researcher who corrects for annotation noise using a pooled confusion matrix may introduce more bias than doing nothing, precisely in the low-error subgroups where original labels were most trustworthy.
23	As LLM annotation pipelines replace manual coding across the social sciences, heterogeneous classification errors will propagate to an increasing share of causal analyses.
24	
25	Several methods address measurement error in downstream statistical analyses, but none handles the specific failure mode we identify.
26	Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI;~\citealt{angelopoulos2023ppi}) and Design-based Supervised Learning~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates by combining predicted and gold-standard labels, assuming homogeneous prediction error across subgroups.

28	Prediction-Powered Conditional Inference (PPCI;~\citealt{sui2026ppci}) extends PPI to conditional means but targets outcome-side prediction error rather than covariate-side misclassification; it corrects $\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$, not the reverse.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
Yet these annotations are not uniformly accurate.
\citet{ashwin2025bias} document that LLM misclassification rates vary by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups defined by refugee status, gender, and education level.
In a pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% binary accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$), within the range assumed in our synthetic DGPs ($\Delta\pi = 0.05$--$0.20$).
When such annotations serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, subgroup-specific errors propagate directly into conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
The resulting bias is not random noise that averages out; it is structured by the same demographic axes that define the research question.
Standard correction procedures, which estimate a single confusion matrix and apply its inverse uniformly, cannot account for this heterogeneity.

We formalize this problem and discover a previously unrecognized bias mechanism.
When a pooled confusion matrix is applied to correct subgroup CATEs, it misattributes error across subgroups with an exact product form: the bias in subgroup $s$ equals $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$, where $\delta_s$ is the deviation from the pooled error rate and $\Delta\tau$ is the CATE heterogeneity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}).
This is not a bound but an exact population-level identity, verified empirically with $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $R^2 = 0.974$ ($K{=}4$).
A direct consequence is that global correction can be worse than no correction at all: in 50\% of our experimental configurations, global correction increases absolute bias relative to the naive estimator, with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest).
Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE) addresses this through hierarchical Bayesian estimation of subgroup-stratified confusion matrices combined with CausalForestDML, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.011 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$).
The bias decomposition identity also yields a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}): a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction will fail (AUC = 0.87), so practitioners can decide whether stratified correction is warranted before estimating any treatment effects.
EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, global correction suffices and EC-HTE's variance cost is not justified (Figure~\ref{fig:bias_mechanism}).

This problem matters because subgroup CATEs inform resource allocation decisions: which communities benefit most from policy interventions, where programs should be targeted, and how reforms affect different groups.
Biased CATE estimates can reverse the sign of apparent treatment heterogeneity, leading practitioners to allocate resources away from communities that benefit most.
The failure mode is subtle: a researcher who corrects for annotation noise using a pooled confusion matrix may introduce more bias than doing nothing, precisely in the low-error subgroups where original labels were most trustworthy.
As LLM annotation pipelines replace manual coding across the social sciences, heterogeneous classification errors will propagate to an increasing share of causal analyses.

Several methods address measurement error in downstream statistical analyses, but none handles the specific failure mode we identify.
Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI;~\citealt{angelopoulos2023ppi}) and Design-based Supervised Learning~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates by combining predicted and gold-standard labels, assuming homogeneous prediction error across subgroups.
These methods produce valid confidence intervals for marginal quantities but do not extend to subgroup-conditional estimands.
Prediction-Powered Conditional Inference (PPCI;~\citealt{sui2026ppci}) extends PPI to conditional means but targets outcome-side prediction error rather than covariate-side misclassification; it corrects $\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$, not the reverse.
\citet{mozer2026ppi} prove that arm-specific rectifiers fix average treatment effect bias under differential prediction error, but their analysis is limited to population averages and does not address heterogeneity estimation.
ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} handles ML-covariate measurement error in regression forests but targets the outcome model rather than the treatment effect heterogeneity structure.
The gap is specific: no existing method corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the one that defines the heterogeneity structure itself, i.e., the effect modifier whose levels index the CATE function.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_bias_mechanism.pdf}
\caption{Bias mechanism under global vs.\ subgroup-stratified correction. Global correction applies the pooled error rate $\bar{\pi}$ uniformly, over-correcting low-error subgroups (introducing bias where none existed) and under-correcting high-error subgroups. EC-HTE matches each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification rate.}
\label{fig:bias_mechanism}
\end{figure}

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item A bias decomposition identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) proving that global correction introduces bias proportional to $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$, with a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}; AUC $= 0.87$) requiring only per-subgroup misclassification rates (Sections~\ref{sec:theory},~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
    \item EC-HTE: hierarchical Bayesian subgroup-stratified confusion matrix estimation, compatible with any CATE estimator (CausalForestDML, R-learner) and composable with PPCI for dual covariate/outcome error ($|\text{bias}|$: $0.179 \to 0.007$), validated across 520 synthetic configurations, a semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment ($N{=}5{,}000$), and four open-source LLMs (7B--9B) confirming $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity on real annotations (Sections~\ref{sec:method}--\ref{sec:multilm_opensource}).
    \item Applicability conditions and crossover analysis ($n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$ for $K{=}2$, $n_{\text{expert}}{=}1{,}000$ for $K{=}4$) establishing when EC-HTE improves over global correction and when it does not (Section~\ref{sec:budget}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We identified an exact bias decomposition identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) showing that global confusion-matrix correction introduces bias proportional to $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$, the product of misclassification heterogeneity and CATE heterogeneity.
This is not a bound but an exact population-level result, and it reveals that global correction worsens subgroup CATE estimates in 50\% of experimental configurations.

Composition with PPCI handles dual covariate/outcome error, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007.

The recommended workflow is straightforward: estimate per-subgroup misclassification rates from a modest pilot sample and check the Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} condition; if any subgroup satisfies $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, apply EC-HTE with $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$ ($K{=}2$) or $\geq 1{,}000$ ($K{=}4$); otherwise, global correction suffices.

When error heterogeneity is low, the variance cost of per-subgroup estimation outweighs the bias reduction, and global correction remains the appropriate choice.

Our validation uses known subgroup structure and primarily symmetric misclassification,
though the product structure extends to arbitrary asymmetric confusion matrices
(Remark~2 and Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}).
Latent or continuous subgroup discovery, online settings with streaming annotations,
and relaxation of the conditional independence assumption are natural next steps.
As LLM annotation pipelines scale across the social sciences, the interaction between measurement error heterogeneity and causal effect heterogeneity will grow more consequential; the broader landscape of error-heterogeneity interactions in automated causal inference remains open.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Measurement error and annotation models.}
Classical measurement error theory shows that correction via estimated error models can amplify MSE when the error structure is misspecified~\cite{fuller1987measurement,carroll2006measurement}; Bayesian approaches require informative priors when identification is weak~\cite{gustafson2003measurement}, and nonparametric methods use repeated measurements or instruments to recover the true distribution~\cite{hu2008nonparametric}.
We formalize this principle for a specific causal estimand: Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} gives an exact identity for CATE bias under global correction with heterogeneous misclassification.
\citet{battistin2014treatment} study treatment effect estimation with covariate measurement error but focus on average effects rather than subgroup-level heterogeneity; \citet{fong2021machine} analyze error propagation when ML predictions serve as regression covariates but do not address the effect modifier setting.
In the annotation literature, \citet{dawid1979maximum} introduced confusion matrix estimation for multiple annotators, with extensions to item difficulty, annotator competence, and hierarchical priors~\cite{passonneau2014benefits,hovy2013learning,paun2018comparing}.
Our hierarchical estimator (Section~\ref{sec:method}) adapts this architecture from label aggregation to causal inference, tying the prior structure to the subgroup dimension that defines treatment effect heterogeneity.

\paragraph{HTE estimation and LLM annotation error.}
Causal forests~\cite{athey2016recursive,wager2018causal}, double/debiased ML~\cite{chernozhukov2018dml}, doubly-robust CATE estimators~\cite{kennedy2023dr}, and meta-learners~\cite{kunzel2019metalearners} all assume that covariates defining heterogeneity are observed without error; when the effect modifier is misclassified, CATE estimates conflate effects across groups.
EC-HTE provides upstream correction that restores valid inputs to any downstream estimator.
The corrected pseudo-outcomes are in principle compatible with other HTE estimators such as the R-learner~\citep{nie2021quasi}.
LLMs now match crowd-worker accuracy on many classification tasks~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp,pangakis2023automated}, but \citet{ashwin2025bias} show that error rates vary by up to $5\times$ across demographic subgroups.
This subgroup-varying error is the failure mode we address: it distorts the very contrasts that define the research question, and prior work documents the pattern without providing a correction mechanism for downstream causal estimands.

\paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}
PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
Applied per-subgroup, DSL operates at the estimand level without cross-subgroup borrowing, yielding strictly higher variance than EC-HTE's measurement-model approach (confusion matrix inversion with hierarchical shrinkage).
\citet{mozer2026ppi} extend PPI to arm-specific ATE correction; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} targets conditional estimands but corrects outcome-side error ($\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$), not covariate-side misclassification; ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} targets the outcome model rather than the heterogeneity structure.
None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification, requiring instrumental variables or partial identification; our problem is structurally distinct because the treatment is observed correctly but the effect modifier is misclassified, admitting exact correction through confusion matrices rather than bounds.
Extended discussion of these distinctions appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.

# LOO-CV AUC Analysis for Prop 2 Diagnostic

## 1. How the old AUC=0.83 was computed

**Source**: `exp005_diagnostic_criterion.py`, function `loso_cv()` (lines 331-350).

**Data pool**: exp001 (36) + exp003 (12) + exp007 (12) = **60 settings, 180 subgroup observations**.

**Label**: `hurts_at_subgroup` = whether global correction has larger |bias_z0| than naive at that subgroup. This is a **different question** from the current `hb_wins` label (HB vs global).

**Diagnostic**: `signed_product` = (pi_bar - pi_s) * Delta_tau.

**Evaluation method**: Despite being labeled "LOSO-CV AUC" in the code output, the `cv_auc` variable is actually the **in-sample (resubstitution) AUC**:

```python
def loso_cv(scores, labels):
    fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(labels, scores)
    cv_auc = auc(fpr, tpr)        # ← in-sample AUC on full data!
    # ... LOO loop below only computes accuracy ...
    return cv_auc, correct / n, ...
```

The LOO-CV loop only produces binary accuracy (with per-fold optimal thresholds), not AUC. The "LOSO-CV AUC = 0.826" reported in the CSV is actually the resubstitution AUC, mislabeled.

**Stored value**: subgroup_auc = 0.8258 in `results/exp005_diagnostic_subgroups.csv`.

## 2. Why LOO-CV AUC = resubstitution AUC for fixed-formula diagnostics

All three diagnostics below are **fixed formulas** computed from known DGP parameters (pi_s, pi_bar, Delta_tau). No parameters are learned from the data:

| Diagnostic | Formula | Parameters learned? |
|---|---|---|
| Delta_pi-only (Prop 2) | max_s \|delta_s\| / ((1-2*pi_bar) * pi_s) | No |
| pi CV | std(pi_s) / pi_bar | No |
| Delta_pi x Delta_tau | max_s \|delta_s * Delta_tau_s\| | No |

For LOO-CV AUC, the "predicted score" for sample i is the diagnostic score. Since the score for sample i doesn't depend on any other sample (it's computed from fixed DGP parameters), leaving out sample i doesn't change its score. Therefore:

**LOO-CV AUC = resubstitution AUC** for all fixed-formula diagnostics.

LOO-CV only matters when the diagnostic involves learned parameters (e.g., logistic regression weights). For the Combined LR diagnostic, LOO-CV AUC (0.830) < resubstitution AUC (0.888), as expected.

## 3. AUC results

### Pool B: 49 settings (exp001=36 + exp003=12 + exp013=1), label = hb_wins

#### Setting-level (n=49)

| Diagnostic | AUC (resub = LOO-CV) | Needs Delta_tau? |
|---|---|---|
| **pi CV** | **0.968** | No |
| **Delta_pi-only (Prop 2)** | **0.889** | No |
| Delta_pi x Delta_tau (current) | 0.889 | Yes |
| Combined LR (resub) | 0.888 | No |
| Combined LR (LOO-CV) | 0.830 | No |

#### Subgroup-level (n=160)

| Diagnostic | AUC (resub = LOO-CV) | Needs Delta_tau? |
|---|---|---|
| **Delta_pi-only (Prop 2)** | **0.865** | No |
| Delta_pi x Delta_tau (current) | 0.726 | Yes |

#### LOO-CV Accuracy (threshold-based, for reference)

| Diagnostic | Setting-level | Subgroup-level |
|---|---|---|
| Delta_pi-only (Prop 2) | 79.6% | 69.4% |
| pi CV | 93.9% | — |
| Delta_pi x Delta_tau | 79.6% | 58.8% |

### Pool B restricted to exp001 only (n=36 settings, 108 subgroups)

| Diagnostic | Setting AUC | Subgroup AUC |
|---|---|---|
| Delta_pi-only (Prop 2) | 0.870 | 0.862 |
| pi CV | 0.958 | — |
| Delta_pi x Delta_tau | 0.870 | 0.683 |

### Pool A: Old exp005 data (n=60 settings, 180 subgroups), label = debiasing_hurts

| Diagnostic | Setting AUC | Subgroup AUC |
|---|---|---|
| Signed product (old) | 0.590 | 0.848 |
| Delta_pi-only (Prop 2) | 0.582 | 0.596 |
| Delta_pi x Delta_tau | 0.590 | 0.469 |
| pi CV | 0.659 | — |

Note: Pool A numbers are not directly comparable to Pool B because they use a different label (global-vs-naive instead of HB-vs-global) and a different data pool.

## 4. Cross-comparison: {diagnostic} x {data pool} x {evaluation method}

| Diagnostic | Pool | Level | n | Resub AUC | LOO-CV AUC | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Signed product (old paper) | A (60 settings) | subgroup | 180 | 0.826* | 0.826* | *Stored value; mislabeled as LOO-CV |
| Delta_pi-only (Prop 2) | B (49 settings) | setting | 49 | 0.889 | 0.889 | Fixed formula |
| Delta_pi-only (Prop 2) | B (49 settings) | subgroup | 160 | 0.865 | 0.865 | Fixed formula |
| pi CV | B (49 settings) | setting | 49 | 0.968 | 0.968 | Fixed formula |
| Delta_pi x Delta_tau | B (49 settings) | setting | 49 | 0.889 | 0.889 | Fixed formula |
| Delta_pi x Delta_tau | B (49 settings) | subgroup | 160 | 0.726 | 0.726 | Fixed formula |
| Combined LR | B (49 settings) | setting | 49 | 0.888 | **0.830** | Learned model; LOO-CV < resub |

## 5. Recommended numbers for the paper

The old paper AUC=0.83 and the new AUC=0.889/0.865 are **not directly comparable** due to three confounded changes:

1. **Different label**: debiasing_hurts (global vs naive) -> hb_wins (HB vs global)
2. **Different data pool**: 60 settings (exp001+003+007) -> 49 settings (exp001+003+013)
3. **Different diagnostic**: signed_product -> Delta_pi-only

For the revised paper, report:

- **Setting-level AUC = 0.89** (Delta_pi-only diagnostic, 49 settings, resubstitution = LOO-CV)
- **Subgroup-level AUC = 0.87** (Delta_pi-only diagnostic, 160 subgroups, resubstitution = LOO-CV)
- Explicitly state these are resubstitution AUC values, noting that for deterministic (non-learned) diagnostics, LOO-CV AUC is identical to resubstitution AUC because the diagnostic score for each observation does not depend on any other observation.

If reviewers press on the LOO-CV vs resubstitution distinction, the defense is:

> "The diagnostic score |delta_s|/((1-2*pi_bar)*pi_s) is a deterministic function of the known misclassification rates, with no parameters estimated from the outcome data. Leave-one-out cross-validation therefore produces identical scores and the same AUC. To confirm, we verified this holds for the logistic regression combined diagnostic (which does learn parameters), where LOO-CV AUC (0.83) is indeed lower than resubstitution AUC (0.89)."

## Files

- Computation script: `compute_loocv_auc.py`
- Summary CSV: `loocv_auc_summary.csv`

3	\subsection{Setup}
4	
5	We evaluate on synthetic and semi-synthetic data generating processes (DGPs); full specifications appear in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.
6	The synthetic DGP generates $N{=}5{,}000$ observations from a randomized trial with $K \in \{2, 4\}$ subgroups, controlled CATE heterogeneity $\Delta\tau$, and subgroup-specific symmetric misclassification rates with heterogeneity $\Delta\pi$.
7	Expert labels ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{50, \ldots, 2000\}$) are a simple random sample with true $Z$ observed; each configuration is repeated for 100 Monte Carlo runs.
8	The semi-synthetic DGP samples $N{=}5{,}000$ tweets from TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, defining $K{=}4$ subgroups by crossing hashtag presence and text length (unbalanced: 39\%/38\%/12\%/11\%), with misclassification rates $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$ reflecting empirical evidence that text features degrade LLM accuracy~\cite{ashwin2025bias}.
9	
10	We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup MLE without pooling), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
11	For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
12	Our Global baseline is equivalent to PPI/DSL~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,egami2024dsl} applied with a pooled (homogeneous) error rate; Stratified MLE corresponds to per-subgroup DSL without hierarchical shrinkage.
13	EC-HTE extends this by borrowing strength across subgroups via hierarchical Bayesian estimation.
14	Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
15	Real-data validation on hate speech detection confirms $\Delta\pi = 0.117$ across text-feature subgroups (Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}).
16	The heterogeneity pattern persists across six OpenAI models spanning three generations (Appendix~\ref{app:multilm}) and four open-source LLMs in the 7B--9B parameter range (Section~\ref{sec:multilm_opensource}).
17	EC-HTE maintains $\geq$94.5\% coverage under up to 50\% subgroup misspecification noise (Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).
18	When empirical asymmetric confusion matrices from the GPT-4.1 pilot are used directly, a subgroup with FNR~$\approx 0.5$ causes EC-HTE to underperform global correction at all budgets (Appendix~\ref{app:semireal}).

20	\subsection{Bias Mechanism Verification}
21	\label{sec:bias_mechanism}
22	
23	The bias decomposition identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) predicts that global correction introduces bias proportional to $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ at the subgroup level.
24	We verify this identity empirically across 520 configurations spanning $K \in \{2,4\}$, two misclassification regimes, and six expert budget levels.
25	Regressing observed subgroup bias on the predicted $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product yields $R^2 = 0.994$ for $K{=}2$ and $R^2 = 0.974$ for $K{=}4$; the residual variance reflects MC sampling noise rather than model misspecification, since Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} is an exact identity at the population level ($R^2 \geq 0.976$ even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$; Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}).
26	In 50\% of configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta_c{=}0$ rows where bias is zero by construction), global correction produces larger absolute bias than the naive estimator.
27	The damage concentrates in low-$\pi$ subgroups: among subgroups where $\pi_s < \bar{\pi}$, global correction increases bias in 84.6\% of cases.
28	Maximum observed amplification reaches 2.86$\times$ (K=2) and 2.41$\times$ (K=4) relative to the naive estimator.
29	Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ amplification surface across the parameter grid.

38	\subsection{EC-HTE Evaluation}
39	\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}
40	
41	Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.
42	In the synthetic DGP with $K{=}2$ subgroups and extreme misclassification heterogeneity, HB EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 (global) to 0.011 (a 5.4$\times$ reduction) while maintaining nominal coverage (0.95) and comparable RMSE (0.093 vs.\ 0.099).
43	The advantage persists at $K{=}4$: EC-HTE achieves $|\text{bias}|{=}0.009$ versus 0.056 for global (6.2$\times$ reduction), though with a small RMSE penalty (0.127 vs.\ 0.125).
44	Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$), methods converge: EC-HTE and global achieve comparable bias ($p > 0.05$; Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}).
45	In the semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment ($N{=}5{,}000$, $K{=}4$), global correction achieves the lowest $|\text{bias}|$ (0.023), while EC-HTE attains 0.027 with higher RMSE (0.225 vs.\ 0.124), consistent with moderate $\Delta\pi{=}0.20$ and unbalanced subgroup sizes (Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}).
46	
47	\paragraph{CausalForest K-dependence.}
48	When the downstream estimator is a CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, the bias mechanism operates with amplified magnitude.
49	At $K{=}4$/extreme/$n{=}500$, EC-HTE Forest reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.191 (global) to 0.040, a 4.8$\times$ improvement with dramatically better coverage (0.91 vs.\ 0.58).
50	The debiasing-hurts phenomenon intensifies: global correction amplifies naive bias by up to 5.9$\times$ in the worst subgroup, because the forest's sensitivity to covariate noise magnifies the effect of label errors.
51	At $K{=}4$/$n{=}100$, EC-HTE Forest RMSE reaches 1.43 (3.5$\times$ naive), underscoring the budget guidelines in Section~\ref{sec:budget}.

82	\subsection{Diagnostic Criterion}
83	\label{sec:diagnostic}
84	
85	Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction increases bias in subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, where $\delta_s = \pi_s - \bar{\pi}$.
86	This condition depends only on per-subgroup misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample, breaking the circular dependency that would arise if the diagnostic required CATE estimates.
87	Since the Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} score is a deterministic function of per-subgroup misclassification rates, a threshold classifier achieves AUC = 0.87 at the subgroup level for predicting whether global correction increases bias relative to the naive estimator.
88	At the setting level, the condition achieves AUC = 0.89 (vs.\ 0.47 for the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product), because it identifies settings where \emph{any} subgroup is harmed.
89	Figure~\ref{fig:roc} (Appendix) shows the ROC curve.
90	
91	\paragraph{Recommended workflow.}
92	\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
93	\item Collect $n \geq 25K / P(Z_{\text{minority}})$ stratified expert labels (e.g., $n \geq 500$ for $K{=}4$, $P(Z{=}1){=}0.2$); compute per-subgroup $\pi_s$ and $\bar{\pi}$.
94	\item Verify (a)~$n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ and (b)~worst-subgroup $\max(\text{FPR}, \text{FNR}) < 0.5$; if either fails, use global correction.
95	\item If any subgroup satisfies $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}), apply EC-HTE; apply PPCI regardless for outcome error (Section~\ref{sec:ppci}).
96	\end{enumerate}

98	\subsection{Expert Budget Analysis}
99	\label{sec:budget}
100	
101	The crossover point at which EC-HTE achieves lower RMSE than global correction is $n_{\text{expert}} = 250$ for $K{=}2$/extreme and $n_{\text{expert}} = 1000$ for $K{=}4$/extreme (Figure~\ref{fig:budget} in the Appendix).
102	Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$), EC-HTE never achieves lower RMSE than global at any budget.
103	HB partial pooling improves over stratified MLE in 21 of 24 configurations, with the two estimators converging by $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$.

105	\subsection{PPCI Complementarity and Estimator Robustness}
106	\label{sec:ppci}
107	
108	EC-HTE composes with PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} for settings where both covariate misclassification and outcome model error are present: EC-HTE+PPCI reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 ($z{=}0$, DGP~C), and the corrected pseudo-outcomes are compatible with other CATE estimators (R-learner bias reduction: 89\%; Appendix~\ref{app:ppci},~\ref{app:rlearner}).

110	\subsection{Open-Source Multi-LLM Validation}
111	\label{sec:multilm_opensource}
112	
113	To verify that misclassification heterogeneity and EC-HTE's correction generalize beyond proprietary APIs, we annotate 500 TweetEval sentiment tweets with four open-source LLMs: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B-IT.
114	Each model independently classifies tweets using a 3-class prompt (positive/neutral/negative); we define a balanced binary label $Z{=}1$ if the true label $\geq 1$ (neutral or positive vs.\ negative), yielding $P(Z{=}1) \approx 0.65$.
115	Per-subgroup confusion matrices are estimated directly from each model's annotations against gold labels.
116	The EC-HTE pipeline---HB confusion matrix estimation followed by CausalForestDML---is identical to the synthetic experiments in Table~\ref{tab:main_results}.
117	All four models exhibit subgroup-heterogeneous misclassification ($\Delta\pi \in [0.125, 0.165]$, $K{=}4$), with consistent subgroup error rankings across architectures (Table~\ref{tab:multilm_cm}).
118	Correction improves 95\% CI coverage from 0.714 (naive average) to 0.941 ($+$22.7 percentage points, $K{=}2$, $n_{\text{expert}}{=}1{,}000$), restoring near-nominal inference across all four models.
119	Under the moderate $\Delta\pi$ observed in these real LLM annotations, global correction suffices for RMSE.
120	Stratified correction achieves lower RMSE than the naive estimator only at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1{,}000$ ($K{=}2$); global correction achieves comparable or lower RMSE than HB EC-HTE at all budgets under this moderate heterogeneity, consistent with the budget guidelines in Section~\ref{sec:budget}.
121	Full per-model results appear in Appendix~\ref{app:multilm_opensource}.
